 Spiking employer healthcare insurance costs near the price tag of a new car

 Full story
 Health insurance open enrollment has begun, and when you sign up for your employer’s plan this year, you might be surprised by the price tag. A new survey shows corporate insurance costs are up by an average of 5%.
 A newly released annual survey from KFF shows the average annual price of employer-sponsored health insurance now tops $28,000 – enough to buy a car. And the share of the cost that’s being passed on to employees has spiked even more.

 Employees are now responsible for paying an average of 9% of the annual cost, putting their annual contribution at $7,471.
 Workers at small companies, those with fewer than 200 employees, were hit even harder by rising costs. On average, workers at small firms now contribute $9,687 a year toward their coverage, KFF reports.
 KFF says nearly 157 million Americans under the age of 65 get their health insurance through their employers. Meanwhile, enrollment in the Affordable Care Act has dropped significantly as the cost for individual insurance has skyrocketed — fewer than 20 million Americans were enrolled in Affordable Care Act health insurance as of February 2026.
 “We have been hearing a lot about Affordable Care Act and Medicaid cuts,” Drew Altman, KFF’s President and CEO, said in a statement. “Now add a 9% increase in what workers with employer coverage paid toward family premiums in 2026 to the reasons voters are so concerned about their health care costs.”
 Artificial intelligence also plays a big role in driving up costs, according to a report from the nonprofit Business Group on Health . The report said hospital systems and medical providers use the technology to maximize insurer and patient billing.
 A recent analysis by Blue Cross Blue Shield said AI billing has added $942 million in extra costs between 2023 and 2025.
 How employers are offsetting higher costs
 With average annual prices on the rise, employers are looking for ways to save . Forty-four percent told KFF they increased employees’ premiums to try to offset increases.

 The average deductible for employees on employer-sponsored health insurance plans is now $1,955 , according to KFF.
 Some are now not only requiring workers to pay a larger share of the premium, but increasing deductibles, as well. They’re also cutting back on some of the drugs and services they cover.
 KFF says a year ago, 43% of employers with 5,000 or more workers covered GLP-1s when prescribed to combat obesity. But in 2026, that dropped to 33% of those large employers covered GLP-1s for obesity. They say most large companies reported that GLP-1 coverage added a significant amount to their overall prescription drug spending.
 More companies are also looking for solutions to save on prescription drugs. Traditionally, they go through pharmacy benefit managers – people who help negotiate rebates and lower prices between employers and drug manufacturers. One in three employers with 50 or more workers told KFF that they offer access to mail-order generic drugs through third-party vendors like SingleCare or GoodRx.

 Worker costs are up

 Small-firm workers pay more

 KFF data shows large employers covering GLP-1 drugs for obesity dropped from 43% to 33% in 2026, and some employers are also raising deductibles and reducing covered services.
